A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NaviAgent, with matching core methods and experiments despite title and formatting changes. The complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V2 reports original ToolBench and API-Bank experiments, component analyses, link-prediction results, and a 60-query evaluation on real APIs in Appendix F.1.

after.justification: V3 retains original benchmark results and reports expanded real-API evaluation, additional component and action ablations, API outage/recovery experiments, and graph-maintenance measurements.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.4 adds periodic probing and reactivation of recovered APIs alongside pruning. The four-action agent, HGT architecture, losses, and search procedures remain substantially unchanged. The three named recovery strategies mainly elaborate v2's existing path-recombination description.

E1.justification: Both versions use ToolBench, API-Bank, and 50 real APIs covering the same seven domains. V3 adds a distinct changing-availability scenario in Appendix F.2, with API outages followed by recovery. The larger real-API query count changes sampling rather than domain or task coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds evaluated ToolNet and ToolPlanner comparisons to both the ToolBench comparison in Table 1 and the real-API comparison in Table 2. These substantially broaden comparison with graph-based and structured planners beyond the retained ReAct, ToolLLM, and alpha-UMI baselines; both added methods were already cited in v2.

E3.justification: The real-API evaluation expands from 60 queries, equally divided by difficulty, to 303 queries comprising 101 easy, 102 medium, and 100 hard tasks. V3 also introduces component-removal controls and a 50-query, two-phase outage/recovery protocol with explicit pruning and reactivation settings. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, and fine-tuning settings are retained.

E4.justification: V3 adds tests separating the effects of bilevel planning, graph access, and search strategy (Table 3); removing clarification and merging retrieval with execution (Appendix H, Table 11); and enabling pruning/reactivation under changing API availability (Appendix F.2, Table 8). These extend the retained TWNM-variant and decision-pattern analyses substantially.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V3's additional results and average timings do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds comparator, ablation, recovery, and maintenance-cost results, including 44.0% versus 48.0% TSR without versus with pruning/reactivation. Real-API NaviAgent TSRs change from 36.7/53.3/63.3% to 37.4/54.4/64.6% across the three backbones under the expanded query set, not identical settings. Retained ToolBench comparison rows, benchmark-variant tables, and runtime values match v2.

T1.justification: New Section 3.4 and Appendix I introduce context-dependent feasible action sets, a KL-minimal projection theorem with a support assumption and proof, an idempotence proposition, a hard-rule corollary, and a possible soft extension. This formal analysis is absent from v2; the existing HGT and loss equations remain mathematically equivalent.

C1.justification: The central bilevel-planning, TWNM, and closed-loop adaptation claims remain. V3 removes the claim to be the first bilevel framework, adds empirical validation as an explicit contribution, and foregrounds live-API generalization. The abstract replaces the 'up to 17 points' headline with an average 13.1-point complex-task gain.

C2.justification: V3 adds a local KL-projection interpretation and explicitly excludes characterization of the full evolving TWNM process. It also interprets the new ablations as complementary component benefits and distinguishes pruning's avoidance of failing APIs from reactivation's recovery of useful tools. Earlier interface, dynamic-environment, and heuristic-runtime limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix E.5 newly documents asynchronous local updates, tool insertion, and offline graph retraining with hot-swapping on a single NVIDIA P40. Appendix C clarifies the retrieval request and illustrates dependency-tree serialization; Table 4 clarifies that the static graph excludes historical invocation data. Existing fine-tuning details and prompts are retained.

R1.justification: V3 removes Qu et al.'s 'From Exploration to Mastery' reference and moderates the first-framework novelty claim. The introduction more explicitly distinguishes action-mode selection from standard planner–executor formulations. Most related-work discussion and cited works remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, baseline description, and results narrative undergo substantial rewriting. Real-API evaluation moves from Appendix F.1 into a dedicated main-text section, and ablations are reorganized. The title and author information change, with acknowledgements and an impact statement added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column preprint layout to two-column conference formatting. Earlier Figures 1–2 are replaced by a conceptual comparison, an architecture/recovery overview, and a redrawn evolution diagram. Comparison tables and plots expand, new ablation tables appear, and the real-API table moves into the main text.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central orchestration and adaptation claims by adding relevant graph-planner baselines and direct component, action, and outage/recovery controls that v2 lacked. The expanded live-API evaluation and maintenance-cost disclosure also improve practical assessment. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses: uncertainty estimates are still absent, and configurations underlying some new ablation rows are not fully reconciled across Tables 3, 4, and 11.
